name: Malic acid

lead: Malic acid is a dicarboxylic acid found in apples and many other fruits that gives them their sour taste. In skincare it is one of the alpha-hydroxy acids (AHAs) used in exfoliating products, usually alongside glycolic or lactic acid.
AHAs are used as superficial peeling agents and to improve the appearance of keratoses and acne, which is how malic acid is used for smoother, clearer-looking skin.

paras: It appears as an ingredient in leave-on and wash-off exfoliants, toners and peels, usually in combination with other acids, applied to the skin in a routine.
A 2018 review notes caution about swelling, burning and itching with AHA products, and says whether AHAs protect against or worsen UV photodamage depends on concentration.

chain: Malic acid exfoliates the skin surface
angle.text: As an AHA, malic acid is included in exfoliants and peels to smooth the surface of the skin. It is usually blended with stronger acids.

lead: Malic acid is a dicarboxylic acid (C4H6O5) produced by all living organisms. The L-form is the natural one, and it gives fruit its sour taste.[1] Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated it from apple juice in 1785, and Lavoisier named it from the Latin word for apple in 1787.[1]

In skincare, malic acid is one of the alpha-hydroxy acids, a group that also includes glycolic, lactic, tartaric and citric acids and is used extensively in cosmetic formulations. AHAs serve as superficial peeling agents and as aids for keratoses and acne.[2] The appearance payoff people look for is chemical exfoliation: loosening dead surface cells so skin looks smoother and more even in tone.[1][3] Malic acid is usually one ingredient in a blend, most often alongside glycolic or lactic acid, rather than the sole active.

Outside cosmetics it is the food additive E296, used for sourness in sweets and snacks and approved in the EU, US and Australia/New Zealand.[1] Gym supplements and pre-workout powders also list it, often as a flavour acid or alongside citrulline as citrulline malate; this is a separate use from skincare.[4][5]

paras: Malic acid has the IUPAC name 2-hydroxybutanedioic acid and exists as two mirror-image forms, L and D. Only the L form occurs in nature, while industrially made material is a racemic mix of both; its salts and esters are called malates.[1] It is the main acid in apricots, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, grapes, peaches, pears and plums, and is also present in smaller amounts in citrus. It contributes to the sourness of unripe apples, and concentrations in fruit fall as it ripens.[1] It is the primary flavour of rhubarb and the tart component of sumac.[1]

Racemic malic acid is made industrially by hydrating maleic anhydride, while the L form can be produced by fermenting fumaric acid.[1] Early commercial supply relied on extraction from apple pomace before synthetic routes took over, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia summary.[6]

AHAs including malic acid are used extensively in cosmetic formulations as superficial peels and to improve the appearance of keratoses and acne.[2] Wikipedia describes AHAs generally as commonly used for chemical exfoliation of the skin, and describes AHA peels as the mildest peel type, used for dryness, uneven pigmentation and acne, with stinging, redness, mild irritation and dryness as possible side effects.[3][7]

In consumer products malic acid appears in toners, exfoliating washes and leave-on treatments, typically listed alongside glycolic or lactic acid. A 2010 post in a T Nation forum tips thread recommends skin products containing alpha-hydroxy acids such as lactic, malic and glycolic acid.[8]

As food additive E296 it supplies tartness, often together with or in place of the less sour citric acid in sour sweets, and it supplies the vinegar-like taste in some savoury snacks.[1] It has about 10 kJ (2.4 kcal) of energy per gram.[1]

In sports nutrition, malic acid is a listed ingredient in some workout powders, and malate also appears as part of citrulline malate. Lifting-forum posts discuss these products, including a 2024 T Nation article thread that describes malic acid as part of an energy-production and recovery stack, and a 2022 thread on a branded workout drink that contains it.[4][5] Proponents of such stacks say malate supports energy metabolism, because malate is an intermediate in the citric acid (Krebs) cycle.[1][4]

A 2016 review of dry mouth (xerostomia) lists malic acid among the options that can ease its symptoms, alongside saliva substitutes.[9] A 2024 randomized clinical trial tested a 1% malic acid spray on diabetes-related dry mouth.[10] A 2023 article in the Mediterranean Journal of Rheumatology discusses malic acid for rheumatic diseases.[11] A 2024 crossover trial in 22 healthy adults examined whether GABA taken with malic acid before a meal affected GLP-1, glucose and insulin responses.[12]

AHAs are organic acids with one hydroxyl group on the carbon next to the acid group.[2] Reviews of their biology describe effects on human keratinocytes, the main cells of the outer skin, and in animal models.[2] In cosmetic practice the result is described as exfoliation: surface cells loosen and shed, leaving smoother skin.[3]

Wikipedia notes that FDA and Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panels have suggested AHAs are safe when sold at low concentrations, at pH above 3.5, and with thorough safety instructions.[3] Its first acid dissociation constant (pKa) is about 3.4.[1]

The 2018 review advises caution about swelling, burning and itching with AHA products, and concludes that AHA effects on skin depend on concentration; whether AHAs worsen or reduce UV photodamage is unclear.[2] Wikipedia reports the most common AHA side effects as mild irritation, redness and flaking, and notes the FDA has warned consumers that AHAs can raise the likelihood of sunburn, an effect reported to be reversible after stopping use.[3]

Wikipedia's chemical peel article notes that professional peels and low-concentration home kits can both cause skin injury, and that the deeper the peel the more complications are possible, including pigment changes and prolonged redness.[7] Chemical suppliers label the pure acid with the GHS exclamation-mark pictogram.[1] Some sour sweets containing it carry warnings that heavy consumption can irritate the mouth.[1]

A review of AHA biology covered effects on human keratinocytes and in animal models.[2] A randomized clinical trial tested a 1% malic acid spray on diabetes-induced xerostomia (dry mouth), which is unrelated to skin appearance.[10] No trial of malic acid alone as a skin exfoliant was found; studies of cosmetic AHAs mostly concern glycolic and lactic acid.

Scheele isolated the acid from apple juice in 1785 and Lavoisier proposed the name acide malique, from the Latin word for apple, in 1787.[1] Malic acid also figured in the discovery of the Walden inversion, a landmark in stereochemistry.[1] FDA and Cosmetic Ingredient Review panels have since suggested safety conditions for AHAs as a group.[3]

Related exfoliating acids include glycolic acid, lactic acid, mandelic acid and citric acid among the AHAs, and salicylic acid among the BHAs.[3][7] Wikipedia's chemical peel article describes AHA and BHA peels as light peels, with TCA and phenol-based peels reaching progressively deeper.[7]
